content: The decision to focus on mental health conditions exclusively was based on two key factors: first, it aligns with the majority of available evidence, and second, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) expressed concerns that lower-income countries may lack the resources to implement such programs for the large number of individuals with more common mental health conditions. No subgroup analyses, such as those based on gender or race, were included. The feasibility of implementing recovery-oriented strategies depends on the infrastructure available in communities. For example, supported employment programs may rely on the broader economic context or the availability of a workforce (both labor and health professionals) to deliver the necessary support. Most of the studies reviewed were conducted in high-income countries in Europe and North America, with a smaller number performed in an upper-middle-income country in Asia. An intersectoral approach is essential to mobilize resources and strategies that promote vocational and economic inclusion. Involving families and communities in recovery-oriented psychosocial intervention programs can be critical for their sustainability. Feasibility may also be influenced by employers’ infrastructure to participate in such programs, as well as the awareness and sensitivity of colleagues and supervisors to reduce workplace stigma surrounding mental health. The GDG concluded that the benefits of recovery-oriented strategies in improving vocational and economic inclusion, as well as obtaining and maintaining employment, outweigh the potential harms, such as dropout risks. While it would have been ideal to apply the recommendations across the spectrum of mental health conditions, most evidence supported benefits for individuals with severe mental health conditions. Both augmented supported employment and standard supported employment showed promise in achieving key outcomes. Recovery-oriented strategies generally outperformed psychiatric care alone in these outcomes. Regarding workplace mental health screening programs, the GDG did not make a recommendation for or against their use during employment due to unclear evidence on whether the potential benefits outweigh the harms. Evidence for pre-employment screening was not considered, as it falls outside the scope of the guidelines. Low-certainty data suggested no significant impact of screening programs on reducing mental health symptoms or improving positive mental health. Very low-certainty data indicated minor, non-significant improvements in work functioning and productivity at five months, which were not sustained at 12 months. There was no significant effect on job satisfaction, and negligible improvements in absenteeism were observed, though one trial suggested a higher likelihood of absence and lower productivity improvement for workers receiving screening programs. The GDG highlighted concerns about confidentiality, the risk of false positives and negatives, and the potential for harm if one-time screening results are inaccurate or misinterpreted. Reporting bias is also a concern, as workers may underreport symptoms due to fears of confidentiality breaches. On balance, the GDG concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against workplace screening programs. The GDG identified several research gaps, including the need for high-quality studies on organizational interventions, cost-effectiveness, and the impact of emerging workplace risk factors. Research is also needed to assess the effectiveness of recovery-oriented strategies for individuals with mild-to-moderate mental health conditions and to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of interventions in diverse workplace settings. Additionally, more studies are required to investigate the effectiveness of manager and worker training programs, particularly in high-risk sectors such as health, emergency, and humanitarian work. The guidelines emphasize the importance of dissemination and implementation. They are available on the WHO website in English, with the executive summary translated into all six United Nations languages. National ministries responsible for mental health and occupational health will be notified through WHO’s regional and country offices, while ministries of labor and employment, as well as worker and employer organizations, will be informed through the International Labour Organization (ILO). A policy brief, developed jointly by WHO and ILO, will accompany the guidelines to facilitate implementation and provide policy options. WHO will monitor the uptake and implementation of the guidelines by reviewing the number of countries that adapt or endorse them. Feedback from implementation activities and stakeholders will be collected to evaluate the guidelines' impact. The guidelines are expected to remain valid for five years, after which they may be updated based on new evidence or other considerations.
